advances: The proposed absolute directional fourth-moment ratio is false even for the specified original entropy rows with positive original transverse and height tilts. The exact deficit multiplicities concentrate the height at its integral mean as the rank increases. This also disproves compact upper bounds on the unnormalized original deficit height parameter and rules out the requested arbitrary-product fourth-moment argument, since a single factor already fails. It does not disprove the closed-halfspace product cap or the locked weak Oertel target.
author: research-agent
proof:
The proof uses only the complete original laws and their exact multiplicities. Abbreviate \(r_m,s_m\) to \(r,s\) while working at one fixed rank \(m\).

First construct the law and verify its entropy characterization. The possible deficit pairs form \(\mathcal T_m=\{(a,y)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2:a+my\le L\}\). There are exactly \(M_m(a,y)=\binom{L-a-my+m-1}{m-1}\) original points above such a pair: they are the complete compositions of \(L-a-my\) into \(m\) parts, as follows by the elementary separator count. The triangle with vertices \((0,0),(L,0),(0,200)\) lies in \(\operatorname{conv}\mathcal T_m\). Since \(1/L+1/200<1\), its interior contains \((1,1)\).

Consider the finite smooth function
\[
F(t,u)=\log\!\left(\sum_{(a,y)\in\mathcal T_m}M_m(a,y)e^{ta+uy}\right)-t-u.
\]
An interior ball of radius \(\varepsilon>0\) about \((1,1)\) in \(\operatorname{conv}\mathcal T_m\) shows that \(F(t,u)\ge\varepsilon\sqrt{t^2+u^2}\): retain a maximizing summand, and use \(M_m(a,y)\ge1\). Hence \(F\) is coercive and attains a minimum. Its Hessian is the covariance matrix of \((A,Y)\) under its positive weights. The support contains \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\), so every nonzero linear functional has positive variance, and the Hessian is positive definite. Thus the minimizer is unique. At that minimizer, both first derivatives vanish. Setting \(r=e^t\) and \(s=e^u\) gives the stated deficit law with means \((1,1)\), and uniquely specifies its two parameters.

Attach the uniform complete-composition kernel at each deficit pair. Exchangeability of the \(m\) parts gives
\(\mathbb E[X_i\mid A,Y]=(L-A-mY)/m\), hence \(\mathbb EX_i=(L-1-m)/m=199\). The multiplicity cancels the kernel denominator, giving precisely the stated original point probabilities. Substitution of \(A=L-\sum_iX_i-mY\) identifies their original exponential parameters as \(\lambda=-\log r\) and \(\gamma=\log s-m\log r\).

For any other law \(Q\) on the original set with full mean \((199\mathbf1,1)\), its slack mean is also one. The expectation of \(\log\Pr(\mathbf X=\mathbf x,Y=y)\) is therefore the same under \(Q\) and under the constructed law \(P\). Consequently \(D(Q\Vert P)=H(P)-H(Q)\ge0\), with equality only for \(Q=P\). Nonnegativity follows directly from \(-\log z\ge1-z\), applied at every point with positive \(Q\)-mass. Equality requires all those ratios to equal one and all of \(P\)'s support to be used. Thus the constructed positive law is the unique entropy maximizer at the original full mean.

We next bound \(r\) without assigning the full means to any conditional row. Given \(Y=y\), put \(B=L-my\). The conditional weights of \(A=a\), for \(0\le a\le B\), are \(w_a=r^a\binom{B-a+m-1}{m-1}\). Their successive ratios are
\(w_{a+1}/w_a=r(B-a)/(B-a+m-1)\).
Since \(\mathbb EY=1\), Markov's inequality gives \(\Pr(Y\le2)\ge2/3\). For every such height, \(B\ge198m+1\). For \(0\le a\le6\), \(B-a\ge24(m-1)\), so the multiplicity ratio is at least \(24/25\).

If \(r\ge2/3\), the conditional weights restricted to \(a\in\{0,\ldots,7\}\) have successive ratios at least \(16/25\). Their mean is at least the mean of the truncated geometric law with that parameter. To justify this elementary comparison, divide the weights by \((16/25)^a\); the resulting sequence is nondecreasing. The covariance of this nondecreasing sequence with \(a\), under the truncated geometric law, is nonnegative, as is seen by expressing twice the covariance as the sum over two indices of the product of their two differences. Normalizing therefore gives the asserted mean comparison. Restoring any masses above seven can only increase the mean.

The truncated geometric mean is
\(g_7(16/25)=16/9-8\cdot16^8/(25^8-16^8)>3/2\).
The last inequality is equivalent to \(5\cdot25^8>149\cdot16^8\), whose sides are respectively \(762939453125\) and \(639950127104\). Therefore \(\mathbb EA\ge(2/3)g_7(16/25)>1\), a contradiction. It follows that \(r<2/3\).

For every height, the same conditional ratios are at most \(r\). The shift inequality \(w_{a+k}\le r^kw_a\), followed by summation, gives \(\Pr(A\ge k\mid Y=y)\le r^k\). Since every conditional support is finite, its mean is strictly smaller than \(\sum_{k\ge1}r^k=r/(1-r)\). Averaging proves \(1<r/(1-r)\), so \(r>1/2\).

For the height marginal define, for \(0\le y\le200\),
\[
B_y=L-my=m(200-y)+1,\qquad
M_y=\binom{B_y+m-1}{m-1},\qquad
H_y=\sum_{a=0}^{B_y}r^a\binom{B_y-a+m-1}{m-1}.
\]
The original height masses are \(p_y=s^yH_y/Z_m\). The rank is at least two, so the binomial coefficient is strictly increasing in its nonnegative budget. It follows, by comparison term by term, that \(H_y\) strictly decreases with \(y\). If \(s\le1/2\), the height weights have successive ratios at most \(s\); the same shift-and-sum argument would imply \(\mathbb EY<s/(1-s)\le1\). Thus \(s>1/2\). Together with \(r<2/3\) and \(m\ge2\), this yields \(r^m<4/9<1/2<s\), proving both claimed positive original tilts.

All multiplicity and curvature estimates below concern the integrated full height marginal. Since the multiplicity decreases with \(a\) and \(r<2/3\), we have \(M_y\le H_y\le M_y/(1-r)<3M_y\). The product formula \(M_y=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(B_y+i)/i\) gives, for every \(1\le y\le199\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{M_{y-1}M_{y+1}}{M_y^2}
&=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\left(1-\frac{m^2}{(B_y+i)^2}\right)\\
&\le(1-1/40000)^{m-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every factor is positive because \(B_y+i>m\), and \(B_y+i\le200m\) on these heights. Hence the factor comparison and its direction hold exactly. The bounds on \(H_y\) now prove
\(p_{y-1}p_{y+1}/p_y^2=H_{y-1}H_{y+1}/H_y^2\le\delta_m\)
at every interior height. The parameter \(s\) cancels in this ratio.

Assume \(\delta_m\le1/4\), and put \(q=p_2/p_1>0\). The exact original height mean implies
\(p_0=\sum_{y=2}^{200}(y-1)p_y\ge p_2\).
The curvature inequality at height one consequently gives \(q^2\le p_0p_2/p_1^2\le\delta_m\), so \(q\le\sqrt{\delta_m}\le1/2\). At all subsequent heights the successive mass ratios are nonincreasing, because their ratio is at most \(\delta_m<1\). Thus \(p_{n+1}/p_1\le q^n\) for \(1\le n\le199\). Combining this with the exact mean balance yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{p_0}{p_1}&\le\sum_{n\ge1}nq^n=\frac{q}{(1-q)^2}\le4q,\\
\frac{\Pr(Y>1)}{p_1}&\le\sum_{n\ge1}q^n=\frac{q}{1-q}\le2q,\\
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}{p_1}
&\le\frac{q}{(1-q)^2}+\frac{q(1+q)}{(1-q)^3}\le16q.
\end{aligned}
\]
The final line uses \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=p_0+\sum_{n=1}^{199}n^2p_{n+1}\), valid because \(\mathbb EY=1\). Since \(p_1\le1\) and \(q\le\sqrt{\delta_m}\), these inequalities prove the asserted probability and variance bounds. The variance is strictly positive because all original height masses, including \(p_0,p_1,p_2\), are positive.

Every possible value of \(Y-1\) is an integer. Pointwise, \((Y-1)^4\ge(Y-1)^2\), so \(\mathbb E(Y-1)^4/[\operatorname{Var}(Y)]^2\ge1/\operatorname{Var}(Y)\ge1/(16\sqrt{\delta_m})\). Because \(0<1-1/40000<1\), \(\delta_m\to0\), proving divergence along ranks for which \(\delta_m\le1/4\).

Finally, \(p_0/p_1=H_0/(sH_1)\le4\sqrt{\delta_m}\). Also
\(H_0/H_1\ge M_0/(3M_1)\ge(201/200)^{m-1}/3\), because \(M_0/M_1=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}(1+m/(B_1+i))\) and \(B_1+i\le200m\). Rearrangement proves the stated lower bound on \(s\), which diverges.

The projection used for the obstruction is the original direction with all transverse coefficients zero and height coefficient one. Its exact conditional complete-composition component is identically zero, so integrating those composition moments cannot remove this failure. The original mean \((199\mathbf1,1)\) remains a legal lattice point, since \(199m+m=L-1\). Products with arbitrary many factors include the one-factor case; therefore no absolute fourth-moment ratio or positive strict-side probability bound can hold throughout the proposed class. The large mass at the equality height explains why this calculation does not itself contradict a cap bound for closed halfspaces containing the mean.
statement:
For every integer \(m\ge2\), set \(h=m\), \(j=199\), and \(L=200m+1=mj+h+1\). Thus \(h\ge2\) and \(L\ge100(m+h)\). On
\[
E_{(L,h,m)}=\left\{(\mathbf x,y)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{m+1}:\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_i+hy\le L\right\},
\]
there is a unique strictly positive entropy-maximizing law with original full mean \((199\mathbf1,1)\). Write its random point as \((\mathbf X,Y)\), and its original slack as \(A=L-\sum_iX_i-mY\). Then \(\mathbb EA=\mathbb EY=1\), and there are unique positive parameters \(r_m,s_m\) such that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\mathbf X=\mathbf x,Y=y)&=Z_m^{-1}r_m^{L-\sum_i x_i-my}s_m^y,\\
\Pr(A=a,Y=y)&=Z_m^{-1}\binom{L-a-my+m-1}{m-1}r_m^a s_m^y
\end{aligned}
\]
on the respective original supports. Conditional on \((A,Y)=(a,y)\), \(\mathbf X\) is uniform on the complete compositions of \(L-a-my\) into exactly \(m\) nonnegative parts. No further slack coordinate is present in this kernel.
Here \(Z_m=\sum_{a,y\ge0:\,a+my\le L}\binom{L-a-my+m-1}{m-1}r_m^a s_m^y\) is the normalizing constant.

Put \(\delta_m=9(1-1/40000)^{m-1}\). The deficit parameter satisfies \(1/2<r_m<2/3\), and \(s_m>1/2\). Consequently the original exponential parameters \(\lambda_m=-\log r_m\) and \(\gamma_m=\log s_m-m\log r_m\) are both positive. For every \(m\) with \(\delta_m\le1/4\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
0<\operatorname{Var}(Y)&\le16\sqrt{\delta_m},\\
\frac{\mathbb E(Y-1)^4}{[\operatorname{Var}(Y)]^2}&\ge\frac1{16\sqrt{\delta_m}},\\
\Pr(Y<1)&\le4\sqrt{\delta_m},\qquad
\Pr(Y>1)\le2\sqrt{\delta_m},\\
s_m&\ge\frac{(201/200)^{m-1}}{12\sqrt{\delta_m}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, the original centered height projection has unbounded standardized fourth moment as \(m\to\infty\), although its mean is exactly the required original integral mean. There is no finite absolute constant bounding all directional fourth-moment ratios in this row class, and the original deficit parameter \(s_m\) is unbounded.
